v.why: Large batches give few updates in 243 epochs, so a larger step compensates for the update deficit.
Under Adam the per-weight step sums over a large fan-in, so wide nets feel larger function-space steps and destabilize sooner.
Steps compound through three hidden layers, destabilizing training at higher rates.
Widening raises the effective step size when the rate is already large, turning extra capacity into divergence.
With tiny rates the net is undertrained and wider layers move the function faster per Adam step.
Stacking layers at a high rate compounds instability and often leaves the net at chance.
Narrow nets have little spare capacity, so extra shrinkage causes underfitting.
With tiny rates the net is update-limited, so fewer updates from larger batches deepen the undertraining.
Larger batches average gradient noise and tame the instability of very high rates.
With many noisy updates per epoch a smaller rate stabilizes training, while at large batches it only slows it.
